'''''Mesembryanthemum''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Aizoaceae]], [[native plant|indigenous]] to southern Africa. As with many members of that family, it is characterized by long-lasting flower heads. Flowers of ''Mesembryanthemum'' protect close at night-time but open in sunlight.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}} Where [[sun]], [[dew]], [[frost]], wind or [[predator]]s are likely to damage exposed [[reproductive organs]], closing may be advantageous during times when flowers are unlikely to attract [[pollinator]]s.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}}

Many ''Mesembryanthemum'' species are known as '''ice plants''' because of the glistening globular bladder cells covering their stems, fruit and leaves,<ref name=WOS>{{cite web |title=Browsing: Aizoaceae |url=http://worldofsucculents.com/?families=aizoaceae |publisher=World of Succulents |access-date=23 June 2017}}</ref> "... they sparkle like ice crystals".<ref>{{cite web |last=Smith |first=Curtis |title=Ice plant |url=http://aces.nmsu.edu/ces/yard/2005/040905.html |work=Southwest Yard & Garden |publisher=New Mexico State University |access-date=25 April 2014}}</ref> In [[South Africa]], Mesembryanthemums are known as "vygies" (from [[Afrikaans]] "[[wikt:vy#Afrikaans|vy]]"), although that term refers to many plants in the family Aizoaceae.

[[Species]] formerly placed in ''Mesembryanthemum'' have been transferred to other genera, such as ''[[Cleretum]]'' and ''[[Carpobrotus]]'', although sources differ.

==Etymology==
[[Jacob Breyne]] coined the name of the flower in 1684, using the spelling ''Mesembrianthemum'' ("midday flower"<ref name=HBSPmes/>), from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] roots {{lang|grc|[[wikt:μεσημβρία|μεσημβρία]]}}, meaning "noon", and {{lang|grc|[[wikt:ἄνθεμον|ἄνθεμον]]}}, meaning "flower", because the species known in his time flowered at midday. In 1719, with the discovery that some species flowered at night, [[Johann Jacob Dillenius]] changed the spelling to ''Mesembryanthemum'' ("flower with the pistil in the center"<ref name=HBSPmes/>), rederiving the first part of the word from Greek {{lang|grc|[[wikt:μεσος|μεσος]]}} ("middle") and {{lang|grc|[[wikt:ἔμβρυον|ἔμβρυον]]}} ("[[pistil]]" or "[[embryo]]"). [[Carl Linnaeus]] used the Dillenius spelling (with the "y") in his description of the ''Mesembryanthemum'' species and the [[International Code of Botanical Nomenclature]] requires the retention of the original, deliberate spelling.<ref name=HBSPmes>{{cite book |last=Jacobsen |first=Hermann |year=1978 |publisher=Blandford Press Ltd. |location=Poole, Surrey |title=A Handbook of Succulent Plants: Descriptions, Synonyms and Cultural Details for Succulents Other Than Cactaceae |volume=III. Mesembryanthemums (Ficoidacea) |page=1257 }}</ref><ref>Oxford English Dictionary Online, s.v. "[http://dictionary.oed.com/cgi/entry/00306549/00306549spg1?single=1&query_type=misspelling&queryword=mesembrianthemum&first=1&max_to_show=10&hilite=00306549spg1 Mesembryanthemum, n.]" (accessed June 24, 2008).</ref>

==Description==
[[Raphide]]s are found in abundance in this genus.{{sfn|Gulliver|1864|p=250}}

==Uses==
Mesembryanthemums are often cultivated as [[ornamental plant]]s for their showy flowers. Ornamental plants may escape into the wild and consequently have become widely naturalized outside their native range. They are considered an [[invasive weed]] in certain places.{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}

==Culture and society==
Some ''Mesembryanthemum'' species are thought to be [[hallucinogenic plants]], like related [[Aizoaceae]],<ref name= "WattPP">Watt, John Mitchell; Breyer-Brandwijk, Maria Gerdina: The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa 2nd ed Pub. E & S Livingstone 1962</ref> and as such may be subject to legal restrictions (e.g., [[Louisiana State Act 159]]).
